report:
**Conclusion: no.** The best placebo-controlled evidence does not show that saw palmetto meaningfully improves urinary symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) over longer follow-up.

Two relatively long, well-designed trials are particularly informative:

- In the one-year STEP randomized trial (225 men, standardized extract 160 mg twice daily), saw palmetto was **not superior to placebo** for urinary symptoms or objective BPH measures.  
  https://escholarship.org/content/qt3d70w83q/qt3d70w83q.pdf

- In the larger CAMUS trial (369 men, 72 weeks), participants received escalating doses up to three times the conventional dose. The average symptom-score difference at 72 weeks was **0.79 points in favor of placebo**; even the confidence limit most favorable to saw palmetto was below a clinically important benefit.  
  https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3326341/?term=%22JAMA%22[jour]

This is important because it addresses a common counterargument—insufficient dose: tripling the dose did not help. Secondary analyses also found no advantage for PSA, a BPH-related outcome.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3979451/

Earlier small trials and older reviews had suggested possible benefit, but larger modern blinded trials have not confirmed it. NCCIH likewise states that saw palmetto has not been shown useful for urinary symptoms related to enlarged prostate. It is generally well tolerated, but tolerability is not evidence of effectiveness.  
https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/saw-palmetto
